newsitem.title: CHINA: Six HK police quit, fear "violating human rights".
newsitem.headline: Six HK police quit, fear "violating human rights".

text.p: Six Hong Kong police inspectors resigned just before the territory's handover to China because they feared receiving orders that would force them to violate human rights, one of the six said on Wednesday.
Four of them quit half an hour before British rule ended at midnight on Monday and Hong Kong became a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China. The other two resigned earlier in June.
"In view of things like the June 4 event, we don't want to serve the Special Administrative Region," former senior inspector Chik Ki-wai told Reuters.

He was referring to Beijing's bloody crackdown on the student-led Tiananmen Square demonstrations on June 4, 1989. Every year since thousands of Hong Kong people have taken part in open-air anniversary vigils in memory of the victims.
Some people fear future June 4 vigils will be outlawed for fear of offending Beijing, although Hong Kong's new leader Tung Chee-hwa has said peaceful demonstrations would be permitted.

"What will happen next June 4? What shall we do?" said Chik. "We are a disciplined force, like the troops and police in Tiananmen. If our boss orders us to shoot, we have to shoot or we'll die ourselves."
He said he would have been put in a difficult situation if ordered to arrest members of Hong Kong's Democratic Party who protested on the balcony of the legislature early on July 1.
"Then what should I have done? Should I have cuffed them? If I had, wouldn't I have become a clown in the eyes of the international community?" he said.
The protest was allowed to go ahead and went off peacefully.
"The problem is that the role of the police is becoming increasingly political," said Chik, a policeman for 21 years. "I don't want to be a politician. I just want to be a policeman."
He said eight officers had planned to resign but two bowed to pressure from their superior and decided to stay.
"We were told to sign reappointment letters or be disciplined. Because of this threat, two of them signed," he said. "This deprived us of our human rights."
"If the police can treat a middle-rank commander like this, can they not be really nasty to ordinary citizens?"

Chik accused the colonial government of racial discrimination because it had barred the six who resigned, all of them ethnic Chinese, from taking early retirement with a pension, an offer extended to their non-Chinese colleagues.
A police spokesman had said the six, as local pensionable officers, did not qualify for early retirement.

Chik said the group planned to take their case to Hong Kong's Human Rights Commission and would sue the British government and the former colonial authority at the International Court of Justice in The Hague.
